title: Suno Studio’s October update meets the work creators already do
question: What changed in Suno Studio’s workflow, and what might it mean for independent musicians shaping their own ideas into a release?
argument: Suno announced changes to clip timing, stretching, and fades. Those controls address editing tasks that creators describe doing, but the supplied accounts do not establish that the October changes improve their results.
synthesis: Suno’s release note identifies the new controls. A practitioner’s video describes cleaning noisy stems in Studio, while Todd Edwards describes generating material to sample. Together, these sources suggest why editable audio matters to musicians with their own production plans. Neither creator is shown testing the October controls, so the sources cannot establish a time saving or quality gain from the update.
limitations: The release note is Suno’s product account. The video follows one creator and includes later mastering outside Studio; Edwards describes his own sampling practice. A direct test of the October controls and a broader range of independent creator experiences are missing.

claims.statement: In its October Studio release note, Suno announced improved downbeat detection, shift-drag clip stretching, and adjustable fade curves, and pop-out windows. Suno describes Studio as its browser-based DAW.

locator.quote: Better down-beat detection
We’ve added a new feature where shift-click-dragging automatically timestretches a clip.
Now, you can shape the curve by dragging the node on the fade icon to create exponential- and logarithmic-shaped fades.
Studio is our powerful browser-based DAW.

We’ve made improvements to the detection of beat 1 in new clip creations. This means the timing of clips and takes on the Studio timeline is greatly improved, and there is more accuracy around the first downbeat in a clip.
You can now pop out the wavetable synth, musical typing keyboard and expanded plug-in views to a floating window that can be dragged around the screen and even onto other monitors.

claims.statement: In a separate Studio demonstration, the video creator said they cut noisy sections from stems, then applied EQ and compression. This documents one editing workflow, not a test of Suno’s October controls.

In a September 29 MusicRadar interview, Todd Edwards described using Suno Studio to generate material for his sampling practice. His account reflects an earlier workflow and does not assess the October update.

locator.quote: While he's initially hesitant to discuss his excitement about the creative applications of AI, Edwards decides it's time to lay his cards on the table, telling us that using AI music platform Suno Studio to generate material to safely sample has reinvigorated his joy in making music.

claims.statement: The announced editing controls appear relevant to creator-led production because one practitioner reports manually cleaning stems and Edwards describes generating audio to sample. This is a workflow inference; neither account demonstrates that the new controls make either task faster or yield a release-ready track.

locator.quote: Improvements to Studio: Tighter timing, clip stretching and fade curves.
using AI music platform Suno Studio to generate material to safely sample

title: What Suno quality tests can actually tell you
question: Which claims about Suno's sound and creative control survive a close look at how creators tested them?
argument: The available tests answer different questions. WaveDisco measured loudness and peaks across a small set of songs and exports. ytyng measured spectral and dynamic properties in exports made from different songs, prompts, and codecs. Two video makers tested how specific inputs shaped particular outputs. Together, they identify useful things to inspect in your own workflow, but they do not establish an overall v6 quality score or a typical result.
synthesis: WaveDisco's same-lyrics, same-prompt comparison is better suited to observing changes among its generated files; its WAV/MP3 result rests on two songs with both formats. ytyng's larger spectral comparison found darker exported v6 files, but different songs, prompts, and codecs leave the cause unresolved. On a Creative Journey's revisions and Andrea Olsen's voice-memo test show why control also needs its own question: did the output follow the intended melody, vocal direction, or arrangement? These sources support testing a creator's actual inputs and exports against separate sound and control criteria. They cannot show that v6 is generally better or worse, or that a prompt change caused every difference heard in one generation.
limitations: The samples are small and none is a blinded listening study. On a Creative Journey acknowledges that repeated generations may explain some perceived improvement; the final version also received Studio editing. Olsen tests one voice memo and sells music education, while WaveDisco and ytyng report their own work. A broader, independent test across genres, prompts, settings, repeated generations, and matched export formats is still missing, as is a wider range of listeners' judgments.

claims.statement: WaveDisco's author used three songs, regenerated each with the same lyrics and prompt across four model versions, and measured LUFS and True Peak. This tests properties of those outputs, not whether listeners prefer them.

locator.quote: Three songs, four model versions each, same lyrics and prompt every time. I measured LUFS and True Peak on every output with the same audio analysis pipeline, and compared WAV and MP3 formats where I had both.

claims.statement: WaveDisco reports no consistent v5.5-to-v6 direction in LUFS or True Peak, but reports that its WAV/MP3 loudness gap disappeared in the v6 comparisons. The author limits the format comparison to two songs.

locator.quote: On LUFS and True Peak, I didn't find one — the numbers move, but there's no consistent direction I can point to.
To be clear: this is two songs where I had format comparisons. It's an illustration, not a study. Your tracks may behave differently.
On v6-mini, v6-wild, and v6: the LUFS difference is zero across all three.

claims.statement: ytyng reports lower high-frequency energy in its v6 exports, while explicitly acknowledging that its pre-v6 comparison used different songs, prompts, and codecs. That prevents attributing the measured difference to the model alone.

locator.quote: v6 was down 2 to 3.4dB at 2 to 12kHz, and the spectral centroid was 36% lower.
The biggest one is that the songs and genres are not controlled. The v6 side is 2 songs and the pre-v6 side is 6 songs, each made from a different prompt.
the v6 side is m4a (Opus 132kbps) and the pre-v6 side is mp3 (about 180kbps VBR), and I compare them as they are.

claims.statement: On a Creative Journey tested increasingly detailed directions for one song and judged a later vocal smoother, but also acknowledged that repeated generations might account for the difference. Its Studio cleanup adds another intervention to the final comparison.

Andrea Olsen of Produce Like a Boss said Suno largely followed her directions and retained the melody of one uploaded voice memo, while she still heard an AI quality in the result. Her channel also promotes her own music-business program, a relevant commercial incentive when weighing her evaluation.

Across the measurement articles and creator demonstrations, a useful release test would separately check the exported file's technical properties and whether the song follows the creator's intended melody and arrangement. This is an inference about a test method, not evidence of average v6 performance: the articles measure different files, and the videos judge individual outputs.

locator.quote: Measurements in this article were taken on three specific tracks using the same audio analysis pipeline on the same day. Suno's output characteristics vary across generations even with identical prompts — these numbers reflect one set of outputs, not a guaranteed behavior of any model version.
Suno's internal master should have more highs than either format, and what I am measuring is only the audio after export.

title: Before releasing a Suno-assisted song, trace what went in and what comes out
question: What should a creator verify before uploading or releasing Suno-assisted work, and what evidence should they watch next?
argument: Start with the creator’s own record: identify the lyrics, melody, recordings and vocals supplied to Suno, then keep the inputs and chosen outputs together. Check the applicable terms and release requirements before relying on any claim about rights. Suno’s account of v6 training, musicians’ concerns about licensing, and an Italian investigation raise separate questions; none determines the rights or reception of a particular song.
synthesis: A practical pre-release check follows from three different kinds of evidence: Zemi describes supplying his own production and vocal before using Suno, a practitioner recommends keeping dated inputs and outputs, and Italy’s competition authority has opened a review of Suno’s terms. Together they support documenting each contribution and checking the applicable terms before upload and release. They cannot establish Zemi’s underlying files, the legal status of any individual song, or the investigation’s outcome. Deezer’s planned filter is a reason to watch future discoverability rules, but the supplied passage does not show that the filter is live or that it covers every AI-assisted release.
limitations: The supplied evidence does not include Suno’s primary terms, a distributor rule for a specific release, or a decision in the Italian investigation. The artists’ accounts and practitioner advice do not verify ownership or resolve copyright questions. Voices still missing include an independent creator who has released a comparable Suno-assisted track and a platform representative explaining how partially AI-assisted music would be classified.

claims.statement: Zemi told Dazed that he produces the beats and toplines, sings, uses Suno to change the voice, and then mixes the result himself; this is his account of his process, not independent verification of each contribution.

locator.quote: “Yes, the voice is AI, but all the rest is produced by me – the beats, the top lines, the production,” Zemi explains. “I sing the songs, bring it over into Suno to change the voice, and then mix it myself. The entire process behind it is human.”

claims.statement: Podcast host Josh of JG Beats Lab advises keeping a folder for each song and identifying which files the creator wrote and which Suno generated. This is a documentation method he recommends, not a legal ruling.

The Italian Competition Authority has opened an investigation into Suno’s terms, including the scope of the copyright license imposed on consumers. Its announcement describes possible unfairness, not an adverse finding; its stated legal frame is Italian consumer and copyright law.

locator.quote: The Italian Competition Authority has launched an investigation into Suno Inc., a US company that provides generative AI services specialising in music creation. The proceedings focus on Suno’s Terms of Service. According to the Authority, the terms under investigation may be unfair pursuant to Article 33 of the Consumer Code since they may create a significant imbalance in the rights and obligations under the contract, to the detriment of consumers.

The scope of the license imposed on consumers as a condition for using the platform services seems to be insufficiently defined, as it is framed in generic and all-encompassing terms, and imposes the waiver of moral rights contrary to Articles 20 et seq. of Law 633/1941.

claims.statement: In response to a new Sony and Universal suit, Suno said v6 training included licensed partner content and community interactions, including creations. The labels’ claims about unlicensed recordings remain allegations contested by Suno.

locator.quote: “v6 was trained on content licensed from our partners, interactions including creations and preference signals from our community, and the accumulated learnings from our team.”Suno
The new complaint filed on Friday, obtained by MBW, accuses Suno of copying 60,202 of the labels’ sound recordings without a license.
“These claims remain fundamentally flawed on both the facts and the law,” Suno said in a statement issued to media, adding that “Suno exists so that more people can make new music.”

claims.statement: The Los Angeles Times reports that participating companies have not disclosed artist payouts or opt-in counts; musicians and songwriter groups question who benefits from the licensing deals. Those concerns warrant watching actual terms and payouts as they emerge.

locator.quote: But so far, none of them have disclosed what artists will be paid, how many artists have opted in, or how much input individual musicians have over whether their work is used. And some musicians and songwriters are fearful of how these AI deals might affect livelihoods.

claims.statement: Andrea Olsen says she uses Suno to explore ideas and does not use its output as her finished product. Her choice describes one producer’s workflow, not a requirement for other creators.

Deezer says it plans a global search toggle for fully AI-generated music before the end of 2026. A creator can watch how Deezer classifies and exposes released music, but the report does not establish that the toggle is live or that it would apply to a particular Suno-assisted song.

locator.quote: Deezer says it is introducing an on/off toggle that will let users exclude fully AI-generated music from their search results.
The French streaming service said on Tuesday (October 13) that the feature will roll out globally before the end of 2026.

claims.statement: Because a creator may supply substantial original material, as Zemi says he does, while Suno may receive material under terms now being examined in Italy, keeping a contribution record and checking the applicable primary terms before upload are prudent steps. These sources do not establish what rights attach to any specific release.

locator.quote: “Yes, the voice is AI, but all the rest is produced by me – the beats, the top lines, the production,” Zemi explains. “I sing the songs, bring it over into Suno to change the voice, and then mix it myself. The entire process behind it is human.”
The contractual provisions on copyright deserve particular attention.
